Draws from the Posterior Distribution of an mvgam Model

Source: R/predict.R
predict.mvgam.Rd

Posterior predictions for mvgam models. type selects the quantity: posterior_predict.mvgam() for "response" (the default), posterior_linpred.mvgam() for "link" and posterior_epred.mvgam() for "expected". "variance" gives the family's conditional variance.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'mvgam'
predict(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  type = c("response", "link", "expected", "variance", "terms", "latent_state",
    "detection"),
  process_error = FALSE,
  incl_autocor = FALSE,
  ndraws = NULL,
  draw_ids = NULL,
  re_formula = NULL,
  allow_new_levels = FALSE,
  sample_new_levels = "uncertainty",
  resp = NULL,
  summary = TRUE,
  robust = FALSE,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975),
  ...
)

Arguments

object

An object of class mvgam.

newdata

Optional data frame with covariates for prediction. If NULL, uses original training data stored in the model object.

type

Character; one of "response" (default), "link", "expected", "variance", "terms", "latent_state", "detection". See Details.

process_error

Logical; if TRUE, the trend adds a sampled innovation to its deterministic submodel. Each posterior draw takes one innovation from the distribution the trend settles into. An autoregressive trend settles into its stationary distribution: an AR(1) draws at \(\sigma^2/(1-\rho^2)\). The Jensen correction on a log link is \(\sigma^2/(2(1-\rho^2))\). A random walk lacks a stationary distribution and a ZMVN() trend lacks dynamics. Both draw their innovations directly. CAR() uses one stationary covariance at every time of an irregular grid and draws from it. If FALSE, the default, the trend contributes its deterministic submodel alone, at its own per-draw values. The argument applies under incl_autocor = FALSE. Conditioning on the fitted state already fixes every innovation.

Each call draws new innovations. Two calls on one fit give different results. Set a seed to reproduce a result.

incl_autocor

Logical; which prediction surface the trend contribution comes from. FALSE, the default, omits the fitted trend[t, s] and uses the two submodels' covariate structure. The effect is the same at the first time point as at the fiftieth. TRUE uses the latent state the model inferred at each time. That is the quantity hindcast() returns. The ELPD is computed from it. loo_R2.mvgam() and bayes_R2.mvgam() request this surface. An R^2 describes the observed series. A row whose time falls outside the fitted grid is refused under TRUE. forecast.mvgam() predicts those times. An in-sample interval under TRUE conditions on states estimated from the same observations. It covers them more often than its nominal level. Calibration is judged out of sample, with forecast.mvgam() or lfo_cv().

The default suits a model whose covariates explain most of the signal. When most of the series-level variation lies in the trend, as in a fit with few covariates and a strong autoregressive process, this surface has little to say. hindcast.mvgam() and forecast.mvgam() are more informative there.

ndraws

Positive integer specifying number of posterior draws to use. NULL (default) uses all available draws.

draw_ids

Optional integer vector selecting a subset of posterior draw indices to use. NULL (default) uses all draws (subject to ndraws).

re_formula

Group-level terms to include: NULL (the default) for every one, NA for none. A formula choosing some of them is not supported.

allow_new_levels

Logical; accepted for brms compatibility. A grouping level the model never saw is refused whatever this is set to. A new level has no fitted random effect. For a new series, it has no latent state to propagate. Predict for levels the fit knows, or refit with the new levels included.

sample_new_levels

Character; accepted for brms compatibility and not used, since new levels are refused. See allow_new_levels.

resp

Character specifying which response variable for multivariate models. NULL (default) returns predictions for all responses.

summary

Logical. If TRUE (the default), returns summary statistics. If FALSE, returns the full matrix of posterior draws.

robust

Logical. If FALSE (the default), uses mean and standard deviation for summaries. If TRUE, uses median and median absolute deviation (MAD).

probs

Numeric vector of probabilities for quantile computation. Default is c(0.025, 0.975) for 95% credible intervals. Can be a single value or multiple values.

...

Unused. Anything passed here is refused.

Value

With summary = FALSE, an [ndraws, nobs] matrix of draws. With summary = TRUE, a matrix with one row per observation and the columns:

  • Estimate: the posterior mean, or the median under robust = TRUE.

  • Est.Error: the posterior SD, or the MAD under robust = TRUE.

  • Q*: one quantile column per value of probs.

A multivariate model with resp = NULL gives a named list of these, one per response.

Details

type selects the quantity returned:

  • "response" (default): draws from the posterior predictive distribution on the outcome scale, from posterior_predict.mvgam().

  • "link": the linear predictor on the link scale, from posterior_linpred.mvgam().

  • "expected": the expectation E[Y | X] on the response scale, from posterior_epred.mvgam().

  • "variance": the conditional variance Var[Y | theta] per draw, from the family's mean-variance relation. It covers the gaussian, student, lognormal, poisson, bernoulli, binomial, negbinomial, gamma and beta families. Other families raise an error. By default the variance is the observation noise around the mean of the two submodels. process_error = TRUE also conditions on each draw's sampled trend innovation.

  • "terms": refused with a pointer to the functions that decompose a prediction. posterior_smooths.mvgam() returns per-smooth draws. fixef.mvgam() and ranef.mvgam() return the parametric and random-effect components.

  • "latent_state": for closure-unit families, the posterior of the latent state of each closure unit given its detection history:

    • nmix(): the latent abundance N given the observed visit counts (Royle 2004).

    • occ(): the occupancy probability P(z = 1 | y_g).

  • "detection": for nmix() and occ(), the per-visit detection probability \(p_{g,j}\) on the response scale.

See also

fitted.mvgam() returns expected values with the inferred trend state. forecast.mvgam() predicts future times from the fitted state. conditional_effects.mvgam() plots predictions against a covariate.

Other predictions: conditional_effects.mvgam(), conditional_smooths.mvgam(), fitted.mvgam(), hindcast.mvgam(), posterior_epred.mvgam(), posterior_linpred.mvgam(), posterior_predict.mvgam(), posterior_smooths.mvgam(), predictive_error.mvgam(), predictive_interval.mvgam()

Examples

# \dontrun{
set.seed(13)
simdat <- sim_mvgam(family = poisson(), n_series = 1L,
                     n_timepoints = 120L, trend_model = AR())
mod <- mvgam(y ~ s(x), trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
              data    = simdat$data_train,
              family  = poisson(),
              chains  = 2, silent = 2)
#> Warning: 9 of 2000 (0.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.

# Predicted counts with their 95% intervals
head(predict(mod))
#>      Estimate Est.Error Q2.5 Q97.5
#> [1,]   1.9970  1.490336    0     5
#> [2,]  14.3895  5.090751    6    25
#> [3,]   7.8510  3.292905    2    15
#> [4,]   8.3570  3.358153    3    16
#> [5,]   4.9305  2.465098    1    11
#> [6,]   7.2530  3.652761    2    15

# The same fit on the link scale, as an expected count and as the
# variance of a count. A Poisson's variance equals its mean.
head(predict(mod, type = "link"))
#>      Estimate Est.Error      Q2.5    Q97.5
#> [1,] 0.655104 0.2437725 0.1550484 1.106528
#> [2,] 2.647316 0.2124152 2.2497025 3.065758
#> [3,] 2.042712 0.1775426 1.7076587 2.390000
#> [4,] 2.099559 0.1963396 1.7273732 2.488058
#> [5,] 1.552701 0.2296787 1.1002138 1.996633
#> [6,] 1.930901 0.3130066 1.3389709 2.536739
head(cbind(
  expected = predict(mod, type = "expected")[, "Estimate"],
  variance = predict(mod, type = "variance")[, "Estimate"]
))
#>       expected  variance
#> [1,]  1.983064  1.983064
#> [2,] 14.446002 14.446002
#> [3,]  7.837157  7.837157
#> [4,]  8.326702  8.326702
#> [5,]  4.850117  4.850117
#> [6,]  7.250155  7.250155

# `summary = FALSE` returns the draws, one row per draw
dim(predict(mod, summary = FALSE))
#> [1] 2000   90

# Next: forecast() predicts beyond the training times from the
# fitted trend state
# }
